reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in GALT, encoding galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase, the second enzyme of the Leloir galactose pathway
Presents in the first days to weeks of life, once milk feeding begins, with poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly and failure to thrive
Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate is toxic to the liver, kidney and brain, while galactitol contributes to cataract formation
There is a strong association with Gram-negative (particularly Escherichia coli) neonatal sepsis, which can be the presenting feature
Untreated infants develop liver failure, coagulopathy, renal tubular dysfunction and a characteristic oil-droplet cataract
Newborn screening and early institution of a galactose-free diet prevent the acute neonatal illness
Despite good dietary control, long-term complications including speech and cognitive difficulties, movement disorder and premature ovarian insufficiency in females still occur
Reducing substances in the urine with a normal blood glucose is a classic clue, but diagnosis rests on enzyme assay and GALT genotyping
reference.pathophysiology: In the Leloir pathway, dietary galactose is phosphorylated to galactose-1-phosphate, which galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase then converts to glucose-1-phosphate and UDP-galactose. In classic galactosaemia the enzyme is deficient, so galactose-1-phosphate accumulates and, together with galactose and its reduced product galactitol, damages tissues. Galactose-1-phosphate is toxic to hepatocytes and renal tubular cells and interferes with several metabolic processes, while galactitol accumulation in the lens draws in water and produces cataract. The mechanisms of the long-term neurological and ovarian complications remain incompletely understood and are not fully prevented by dietary treatment.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal hepatitis and biliary or metabolic liver disease
Tyrosinaemia type 1 and other metabolic hepatopathies
Other causes of neonatal cholestasis and conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
additionalInvestigations: Newborn screening result and erythrocyte GALT enzyme activity assay
Urine testing for reducing substances (non-glucose) with paired blood glucose
Liver function tests and coagulation studies
Ophthalmological examination for cataract and renal tubular function assessment
redFlags: Neonatal jaundice, hepatomegaly and poor feeding after milk introduction
Escherichia coli or other Gram-negative sepsis in a young infant
reference.prognosis: A galactose-free diet started early prevents the life-threatening neonatal illness and reverses the acute hepatic, renal and cataract manifestations. However, long-term outcomes remain guarded, with a substantial proportion developing cognitive, speech and motor difficulties, and most females experiencing premature ovarian insufficiency despite adherence.
pitfalls: Waiting for newborn screening results before treating a clinically unwell infant
Missing associated Gram-negative sepsis, which requires urgent antibiotic treatment
Assuming strict dietary control prevents all long-term complications
Overlooking the diagnosis when urine glucose oxidase dipstick is negative despite positive reducing substances
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Lifelong strict galactose-free diet begun as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, eliminating lactose-containing milk and substituting a soya-based formula
Prompt sepsis workup and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Escherichia coli in the acutely ill neonate
Supportive treatment of liver failure, coagulopathy and renal tubular dysfunction during the acute presentation
Ophthalmological review for the characteristic oil-droplet cataract, which typically resolves with dietary galactose restriction
Dietetic supervision to secure adequate calcium and vitamin D intake and long-term monitoring of bone health
Long-term follow-up for cognitive, speech and motor difficulties and, in females, endocrine surveillance and management of primary ovarian insufficiency
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with cascade testing of the family
Coordinated multidisciplinary care through metabolic medicine and clinical genetics
